claims.text: Simultaneous DSC and high-throughput in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction can accurately determine melting temperatures across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The combined method can accurately determine enthalpy and entropy of fusion across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The combined method can accurately determine volume changes at melting across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The combined method can accurately determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The simultaneous method is efficient and high-throughput.
Preparing alloys in a controlled, homogenized state minimizes inhomogeneities before measurement.
An inert atmosphere or vacuum prevents oxidation during the measurements.
Suitable controlled heating rates are 5–20 °C/min.
Time synchronization of DSC and diffraction data enables correlation of thermal and structural transitions.
Real-time phase information from X-ray diffraction enables heat-flow anomalies to be assigned to structural transitions such as melting onset and volume expansion.
Integration of DSC heat-flow signals yields enthalpy and entropy changes.
In-situ X-ray diffraction monitors the onset of crystallographic disorder and lattice-parameter changes.
Crystallographic disorder and lattice-parameter changes can be used to extract melting temperature and volume change at melting.
Combining DSC and diffraction mitigates ambiguities associated with either technique alone by independently validating thermal and structural melting endpoints.
The integrated methodology will achieve approximately ±1–2% accuracy relative to conventional benchmarks.
Standard DSC or conventional high-temperature diffraction alone often has difficulty distinguishing melting onset from overlapping thermal events and lacks structural context.
The approach may be less applicable to alloys that decompose or exhibit sluggish kinetics before melting.
Highly reactive liquid phases may interfere with synchrotron data collection.
Temperature-dependent heat-capacity measurements can provide liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
A deviation greater than ±2% from independent conventional measurements for any key property would falsify the claimed accuracy of the integrated approach.
